title: Abraham Lincoln
summary: The 16th president of the United States (1861–1865), an Illinois lawyer and Republican who led the Union through the Civil War, issued the Emancipation Proclamation, backed the Thirteenth Amendment, and was assassinated in April 1865.

review.question: Why did Lincoln win the presidency in 1860 with less than 40 percent of the popular vote?
review.answer: Four major candidates split the vote; Lincoln carried every free state, which gave him 180 of 303 electoral votes, a clear Electoral College majority, even though he was not on the ballot in much of the South.

review.question: How did the actions of enslaved people shape Lincoln's emancipation policy, according to historians such as Ira Berlin?
review.answer: By fleeing to Union lines and offering labor and military service, enslaved people forced Union officers, Congress and the president to decide their status; Lincoln, who had first favored gradual, compensated emancipation and colonization, moved toward the Emancipation Proclamation as that pressure grew.

review.question: Why do historians debate Lincoln's title of "Great Emancipator"?
review.answer: Some see his leadership as the decisive force that ended slavery, while others argue he was a reluctant emancipator and that enslaved people were the prime movers; the debate is about how to weigh presidential leadership against the agency of the enslaved.

timeline.event: Born near Hodgenville, Kentucky.
First elected to the Illinois legislature.
As a first-term Whig congressman, introduces the Spot Resolutions challenging the case for war with Mexico.
Gives the "House Divided" speech; later loses the Senate race to Stephen A. Douglas.
Elected 16th president with a majority of electoral votes from the free states.
Inaugurated after seven Southern states had seceded.
Thirty-eight Dakota men are hanged at Mankato after Lincoln commutes most of the death sentences.
The Emancipation Proclamation takes effect in areas in rebellion.
Delivers the Gettysburg Address.
Reelected president.
Shot by John Wilkes Booth at Ford's Theatre; dies the next morning.

misconception.myth: Lincoln dashed off the Gettysburg Address on the back of an envelope on the train to Gettysburg.
misconception.fact: Lincoln worked on the speech in the weeks before November 19, 1863; a Library of Congress copy begins in ink on Executive Mansion stationery written in Washington, and the drafts are in steady handwriting unlike a moving train's.
misconception.why: The envelope story turns a carefully revised speech into a lucky improvisation and hides how deliberately Lincoln shaped his public words.

title: American Civil War
summary: The war of 1861–1865 between the United States and eleven slaveholding Southern states that seceded to form the Confederacy; it preserved the Union and destroyed slavery at a cost of roughly 750,000 lives.

review.question: Why did Deep South states secede after the 1860 election, before Lincoln had taken office?
review.answer: They saw the victory of a party opposed to slavery's expansion as a threat to slavery itself. Mississippi's declaration said its position was thoroughly identified with slavery, and South Carolina's centered on Northern refusal to return fugitives from slavery.

review.question: How did enslaved people help turn a war for the Union into a war against slavery?
review.answer: By fleeing to Union lines from 1861 on, they forced the army and Congress to decide their status, which led to contraband policy, the Confiscation Acts, abolition in Washington, D.C., the Emancipation Proclamation, and the enlistment of about 179,000 Black soldiers.

review.question: Why do historians now cite about 750,000 deaths instead of the long-used 620,000?
review.answer: J. David Hacker compared census survival rates for 1860–1870 with the decades before and after, and the shortfall pointed to about 750,000 deaths (range 650,000–850,000), since earlier counts relied on incomplete military records.

timeline.event: A South Carolina convention votes 169 to 0 to secede after Abraham Lincoln's election.
Delegates from seven seceded states meet in Montgomery, Alabama, and choose Jefferson Davis as Confederate president.
Confederate forces fire on Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor; it surrenders the next day and Lincoln calls for 75,000 volunteers.
At Fort Monroe, General Benjamin Butler begins receiving people fleeing slavery as "contraband of war."
Congress abolishes slavery in the District of Columbia.
The Battle of Antietam, the bloodiest single day in American history, gives Lincoln the victory he awaited to announce emancipation.
The Emancipation Proclamation takes effect in areas under Confederate control.
The War Department creates the Bureau of Colored Troops to organize Black regiments.
Pickett's Charge fails, ending the three-day Battle of Gettysburg.
Vicksburg surrenders to Ulysses S. Grant, splitting the Confederacy in two.
Congress grants Black soldiers pay equal to white soldiers, retroactively.
William T. Sherman's army captures Atlanta before marching to the sea.
Robert E. Lee surrenders the Army of Northern Virginia to Grant at Appomattox.

misconception.myth: The Civil War was fought over states' rights or tariffs, not slavery.
misconception.fact: The seceding states said otherwise at the time. Mississippi declared its position "thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery," South Carolina complained that Northern states would not enforce the Fugitive Slave Act, and Confederate Vice President Alexander Stephens rested the new government on Black inequality. The only state right at stake was the right to protect slavery.
misconception.why: The postwar "Lost Cause" story recast secession as a defense of constitutional principle. Believing it hides what the war was about and why emancipation and the Reconstruction amendments followed from it.

title: Articles of Confederation
aliases: Articles of Confederation and Perpetual Union
summary: The first written frame of national government for the United States, adopted by the Second Continental Congress on November 15, 1777, in force from Maryland's ratification on March 1, 1781, until the Constitution replaced it in 1789; it joined sovereign states in a league governed by a one-state, one-vote Congress with no power to tax.

review.question: Why did Congress under the Articles struggle to pay its bills, and what did that mean in practice?
review.answer: The Articles gave Congress no power to tax; it could only ask the state legislatures for money, and between 1781 and 1787 it received about $1.5 million of the $10 million it requested, leaving it unable to pay war debts or raise its own army, as Shays' Rebellion showed.

review.question: How did the dispute over western lands delay the Articles from taking effect?
review.answer: Ratification had to be unanimous, and states without western land claims, above all Maryland, refused to ratify until states such as Virginia gave up their claims; Maryland ratified only on March 1, 1781, after Virginia agreed to do so.

review.question: How did the Articles' clause on Indian affairs lead to conflict at Fort Stanwix in 1784?
review.answer: The Articles gave Congress power over affairs with Native peoples who were not members of any state, but New York claimed the Haudenosaunee as within its jurisdiction and held its own meeting, so Congress and the state competed for land cessions, and New York later sold land it had failed to obtain by treaty.

review.question: Why did the framers of the Articles deliberately create a weak central government?
review.answer: Many Americans feared losing power to a central body, as the earlier failure of the Albany Plan showed, so the Articles let each state keep its sovereignty and every power not expressly delegated, gave Congress no taxing power and no independent executive or courts, and required every state to agree to amendments.

timeline.event: After the Lee Resolution, the Second Continental Congress appoints a committee, one member per colony, to plan a confederation.
The committee, with John Dickinson as principal writer, presents its draft to Congress.
After debate sharpened by the British capture of Philadelphia, Congress adopts the Articles.
Congress sends the Articles to the states, all thirteen of which must ratify.
Virginia becomes the first state to ratify.
New Jersey ratifies after holding out over western land claims.
Delaware ratifies, leaving Maryland the last holdout.
Congress creates a Department of Foreign Affairs.
Maryland ratifies after Virginia agrees to give up its western claims; the Articles take effect.
Confederation commissioners impose the Treaty of Fort Stanwix on Haudenosaunee delegates while New York pursues its own negotiations.
Delegates from several states gather at the Annapolis Convention.
New York's refusal of the revised impost ends Congress's attempt to win a national tariff.
The Constitutional Convention meets in Philadelphia to revise the Articles and instead drafts a new constitution.
The Articles cease to be in force as government under the Constitution begins.

misconception.myth: The government under the Articles of Confederation accomplished nothing and was simply a failure.
misconception.fact: Despite having no power to tax, the Confederation Congress saw the Revolutionary War to its end with the 1783 Treaty of Paris, set up departments of Foreign Affairs, War, Marine and Treasury, and passed the Land Ordinances of 1784 and 1785 and the Northwest Ordinance of 1787, which created a process for admitting new states on equal terms with the original thirteen.
misconception.why: Because the Constitution replaced the Articles, the Confederation is often remembered only as the failed first draft, a view that overlooks lasting achievements and the real reasons people in the 1770s distrusted a strong central government.

title: Brown v. Board of Education
aliases: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka
summary: The unanimous 1954 U.S. Supreme Court decision holding that state laws segregating public schools by race violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, rejecting the "separate but equal" doctrine in public education.

review.question: Why did the NAACP's lawyers value the Kansas case even though Topeka's Black and white schools were roughly comparable in buildings and resources?
review.answer: Because the facilities were substantially comparable, the Kansas case forced the Court to decide whether segregation itself was unconstitutional rather than merely ordering states to equalize unequal schools, and it showed that school segregation was a national issue and not only a Southern one.

review.question: Why was the District of Columbia case, Bolling v. Sharpe, decided separately from the four state cases?
review.answer: The Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause restrains the states, not the federal government, so segregation in the federal capital had to be challenged under the Fifth Amendment instead.

review.question: How did the Court's approach to remedies allow segregation to continue for years after 1954?
review.answer: The 1954 ruling did not say how or when schools must desegregate; Brown II in 1955 left it to federal district courts to proceed "with all deliberate speed," and opponents used that vague standard to delay, admit only token numbers of Black students, pass new segregation laws, or, as in Prince Edward County, close public schools from 1959 to 1964.

timeline.event: Students led by 16-year-old Barbara Rose Johns walk out of the overcrowded Robert Russa Moton High School in Farmville, Virginia.
NAACP lawyers file Davis v. County School Board of Prince Edward County, later joined to Brown.
The Supreme Court hears the first arguments in the consolidated school cases.
Reargument begins on questions the Court posed, including the history of the Fourteenth Amendment and possible remedies.
The Court rules unanimously that segregated public schools violate the Equal Protection Clause; Bolling v. Sharpe is decided the same day.
In Brown II the Court orders desegregation to proceed with all deliberate speed under federal district courts.
The Southern Manifesto denouncing the decision is introduced in Congress.
Prince Edward County, Virginia, cuts off public school funding rather than desegregate.
Prince Edward County's public schools reopen after the Supreme Court's Griffin decision.
Attorneys ask the federal court to reopen the Topeka case to test whether segregation's effects remained (Brown III).

misconception.myth: The case began when Oliver Brown alone sued after his daughter Linda was turned away from a nearby white school and forced to walk far to a Black school.
misconception.fact: The Topeka NAACP deliberately organized a class action with 13 parents on behalf of 20 children; Oliver Brown was recruited to join and named because he was the only man in the group, and the Supreme Court decided Kansas's case together with cases from South Carolina, Virginia, Delaware and the District of Columbia involving nearly 200 people.
misconception.why: Reducing Brown to one family's story hides the years of organized legal strategy and the many students, parents, teachers and lawyers, in the South and beyond it, who took risks to bring the cases.

title: Constitutional Convention
summary: The meeting of delegates from twelve states in Philadelphia from May 25 to September 17, 1787, that was called to revise the Articles of Confederation and instead drafted the United States Constitution.

review.question: Why did the convention end up writing a whole new constitution when Congress had asked only for revisions?
review.answer: Many delegates believed the Articles left the central government too weak; Randolph's Virginia Plan on May 29 proposed a new national legislature, executive and judiciary, and by mid-June the delegates had accepted that they were drafting a new frame of government rather than amending the old one.

review.question: How did the Great Compromise settle the quarrel between large and small states?
review.answer: It gave the House of Representatives seats in proportion to each state's population and gave every state equal representation in the Senate; it passed on July 16, 1787, by a single state's margin.

review.question: How did the convention's decisions strengthen slaveholding states?
review.answer: Counting three-fifths of enslaved people added to slave states' seats in the House and, through the electoral college, their weight in presidential elections; the convention also barred Congress from ending the Atlantic slave trade before 1808 and added a fugitive slave clause.

review.question: Why do historians disagree about whether the Constitution was a proslavery document?
review.answer: Paul Finkelman argues its many protections for slavery made it a proslavery bargain, while Sean Wilentz argues that by refusing to recognise property in people the framers left an opening later antislavery politicians used; critics of Wilentz note that his key Madison quotation may have been added to Madison's notes later.

timeline.event: The Confederation Congress calls a convention to meet in Philadelphia in May to revise the Articles of Confederation.
The convention's scheduled opening day; too few delegations are present, so members adjourn from day to day.
Seven states form a quorum and the delegates unanimously elect George Washington president of the convention.
Edmund Randolph presents the Virginia Plan, and the convention adopts a rule keeping its proceedings secret.
James Wilson and Charles Pinckney propose counting three-fifths of enslaved people for representation.
The convention adopts the three-fifths rule, six states to two with two divided.
The Great (Connecticut) Compromise passes by a margin of one state.
A bargain between New England and Deep South delegates protects the Atlantic slave trade until 1808.
Thirty-eight delegates sign thirty-nine names to the finished Constitution; three present delegates refuse.
Congress unanimously resolves to send the Constitution to the states for ratifying conventions.
Delaware becomes the first state to ratify.
New Hampshire becomes the ninth state to ratify, enough for the Constitution to take effect.

misconception.myth: The delegates were sent to Philadelphia to write a new constitution.
misconception.fact: Congress called the meeting only to revise the Articles of Confederation and report proposed alterations to Congress and the states; the delegates decided on their own, by mid-June 1787, to draft an entirely new frame of government, and their Constitution took effect once nine state conventions had ratified it.
misconception.why: Because the convention's product replaced the Articles completely and is commemorated on September 17, it is easy to assume a new constitution was the assignment from the start, which hides how bold, and how contested, the delegates' decision was.

title: Declaration of Independence
aliases: The unanimous Declaration of the thirteen united States of America
summary: The statement adopted by the Second Continental Congress on July 4, 1776, announcing that the thirteen American colonies were free and independent states, setting out a philosophy of natural rights and government by consent, and listing grievances against King George III.

review.question: Why did Congress cut Jefferson's passage blaming the king for the slave trade?
review.answer: Jefferson recorded that it was struck to accommodate South Carolina and Georgia, which wanted the slave trade to continue, and that some Northern delegates were uneasy because Northern merchants had carried enslaved people; the deletion kept those delegations behind independence.

review.question: How did declaring independence help the American war effort abroad?
review.answer: France would consider a formal alliance only once the colonies declared independence, so the Declaration opened the way to recognition and to the 1778 Treaty of Alliance with France, followed by Dutch recognition in 1782 and British acknowledgement in the 1783 Treaty of Paris.

review.question: Why is July 4 not the day the Declaration was signed?
review.answer: July 4 was the day Congress approved the text; the signing copy was only ordered on July 19, and most delegates signed it on August 2, 1776, with others signing later.

review.question: How did later reformers use the Declaration's language?
review.answer: The women who met at Seneca Falls in 1848 modelled their Declaration of Sentiments on it, declaring that all men and women are created equal, and Frederick Douglass in 1852 measured the nation's celebration of independence against the slavery it still allowed.

timeline.event: Richard Henry Lee of Virginia moves in Congress that the colonies are, and ought to be, free and independent states.
The drafting committee presents Jefferson's draft, edited by Adams and Franklin, to Congress.
A first vote on Lee's resolution: nine colonies in favour, Pennsylvania and South Carolina opposed, Delaware deadlocked and New York abstaining.
Twelve colonies vote for independence, with New York abstaining.
Congress approves the revised text and orders it printed; John Dunlap prints about 200 broadsides.
John Nixon gives the first public reading in the State House Yard in Philadelphia.
Congress orders the text engrossed on parchment under a new title for members to sign.
John Hancock and most of the delegates sign the engrossed parchment.
Congress authorizes a printing that carries the signers' names for the first time.

misconception.myth: The delegates signed the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776.
misconception.fact: Congress approved the text on July 4, but it ordered a parchment copy for signing only on July 19; most delegates signed on August 2, 1776, a few signed later that year, and Thomas McKean signed sometime after January 1777.
misconception.why: Later recollections by Jefferson and Adams placed the signing on July 4, and the copies printed that week carried only the names of John Hancock and Charles Thomson, so the date of approval and the act of signing blurred together in popular memory.

title: Equal protection
summary: The constitutional guarantee, in the Fourteenth Amendment's command that no state "deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws," that government may not draw arbitrary or invidious distinctions among the people it governs.

review.question: Why did the framers of the Fourteenth Amendment write an equal protection guarantee into the Constitution rather than rely on ordinary legislation?
review.answer: They wanted to give civil rights measures such as the Civil Rights Act of 1866 a constitutional footing that a later simple majority in Congress could not repeal, so that the equal legal standing of formerly enslaved people could not be undone by shifting politics.

review.question: How can two laws that both classify people be judged so differently under the Equal Protection Clause?
review.answer: Courts apply different levels of review depending on the classification. Most laws need only a rational relationship to a legitimate interest, but a law that sorts people by race (a suspect classification) or burdens a fundamental right must survive strict scrutiny, meaning it must be narrowly tailored to a compelling government interest.

timeline.event: The House approves the proposed Fourteenth Amendment, 120-32, carrying the equal protection language.
Ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment writes the Equal Protection Clause into the Constitution.
The Slaughter-House Cases recognize formerly enslaved African Americans as the clause's primary intended beneficiaries while noting its words reach everyone.
Yick Wo v. Hopkins applies equal protection beyond race to discriminatory enforcement of an ordinance.
Brown v. Board of Education holds that segregated public schools violate equal protection.
Reed v. Reed applies heightened review to a sex-based classification for the first time.
Craig v. Boren sets the intermediate-scrutiny standard for sex classifications.
Obergefell v. Hodges holds that state bans on same-sex marriage violate the clause.

misconception.myth: The Equal Protection Clause forbids government from ever treating people differently.
misconception.fact: Governments classify people constantly, by age, income, or occupation, and most such lines stand if they are "rationally related to a legitimate state interest"; only suspect classifications such as race, or laws burdening fundamental rights, face the demanding test of strict scrutiny.
misconception.why: Equal protection requires equal treatment of those who are "similarly situated," not identical treatment of everyone, so the real question a court asks is which differences a law may lawfully draw on.

title: Fifteenth Amendment
aliases: Fifteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution
summary: The 1870 amendment to the U.S. Constitution that bars the United States and the states from denying or abridging citizens' right to vote "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude," and gives Congress power to enforce that ban; the last of the three Reconstruction Amendments.

review.question: Why could Southern states keep most Black men from voting for decades even though the Fifteenth Amendment was in force?
review.answer: The amendment only barred denial of the vote on account of race, color or previous servitude and left states free to set other qualifications, so states used poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses and discriminatory administration, while 1876 Supreme Court rulings such as United States v. Reese weakened federal enforcement.

review.question: How did the amendment divide the women's rights movement?
review.answer: Because it protected against racial but not sex discrimination, Lucy Stone and Frederick Douglass supported it as a first step while Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony opposed any amendment that excluded women; the American Equal Rights Association broke up in 1869 and two rival suffrage organizations formed.

review.question: How is the Voting Rights Act of 1965 connected to the Fifteenth Amendment?
review.answer: The Act used the enforcement power in the amendment's Section 2; President Johnson asked Congress for a law that would make it impossible to thwart the amendment, and the Act abolished remaining barriers and authorized federal supervision of registration.

timeline.event: Congress enfranchises Black men in the District of Columbia and the territories and requires seceded states to guarantee Black male suffrage as a condition of readmission.
Representative George Boutwell proposes a suffrage amendment in the House.
After a conference committee narrows the text to racial discrimination, Congress gives final approval (House 144 to 44, Senate 39 to 13).
The American Equal Rights Association splits over the amendment's omission of women at its annual meeting.
The amendment is ratified by three-fourths of the states.
Black Baltimoreans hold a parade celebrating ratification.
United States v. Reese and United States v. Cruikshank narrow federal enforcement.
Southern states begin adopting grandfather clauses that exempt mostly white voters from literacy tests.
Guinn v. United States unanimously strikes down Oklahoma's grandfather clause.
Lane v. Wilson holds that the amendment reaches subtle as well as overt discrimination.
President Lyndon B. Johnson asks Congress for a law to make the amendment impossible to evade.
Rice v. Cayetano holds that the amendment protects all persons and that ancestry can serve as a proxy for race.
The Supreme Court strikes down a key federal oversight provision of the Voting Rights Act.

misconception.myth: The Fifteenth Amendment gave all Black Americans the right to vote in 1870.
misconception.fact: The amendment only forbade denying the vote because of race, color or previous servitude; it conferred no right of suffrage on anyone, did not cover sex, so Black women were still excluded, and left states free to impose poll taxes, literacy tests and other qualifications that Southern states used to disfranchise most Black men until federal enforcement under the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
misconception.why: Treating 1870 as the moment Black Americans won the vote hides nearly a century of disfranchisement and explains poorly why the civil rights movement still had to fight for the ballot in the 1960s.

title: Fourteenth Amendment
aliases: Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution
summary: The 1868 amendment to the U.S. Constitution that made all persons born or naturalized in the United States citizens and barred states from denying any person due process of law or the equal protection of the laws; it also reshaped representation, barred certain former officials who joined the rebellion from office, and settled Civil War debts.

review.question: What problems was the amendment meant to solve after the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery?
review.answer: Southern states were passing Black Codes to limit freed people's rights while white southerners terrorized them, and Dred Scott's rule still denied Black Americans citizenship; the amendment made all persons born or naturalized in the country citizens, barred states from denying due process or equal protection, and gave Congress power to enforce those guarantees.

review.question: How did the Slaughter-House Cases change what the amendment meant in practice?
review.answer: The Court held that the Privileges or Immunities Clause protected only rights of national citizenship, leaving most rights to the states and turning the clause into a practical nullity, so later protection of Bill of Rights guarantees against the states came instead through the Due Process Clause, case by case.

review.question: Why were former Confederate states required to ratify the amendment?
review.answer: White southerners rejected it almost unanimously in 1866 and 1867; after Northern voters backed Republicans in the 1866 elections, Congress made ratification a condition for restoring a state's representation, and Southern ratifications in 1868 completed the three-fourths.

review.question: Who was left out of the citizenship clause at first, and how did that change?
review.answer: Native people under tribal rather than U.S. authority were excluded, and Elk v. Wilkins (1884) held that Native Americans were not U.S. citizens even after leaving their nations; Congress made all Native Americans citizens only with the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924.

timeline.event: Congress creates the Joint Committee of Fifteen on Reconstruction.
Congress passes the Civil Rights Act of 1866.
The Senate passes the amendment, 33 to 11.
The House passes the amendment, 120 to 32.
The joint resolution is submitted to the states.
The Reconstruction Act places former Confederate states except Tennessee under military districts.
Louisiana and South Carolina ratify, completing the three-fourths needed.
Secretary of State William H. Seward certifies ratification by 28 states.
The Slaughter-House Cases narrow the Privileges or Immunities Clause.
Minor v. Happersett holds that citizenship does not carry a right to vote.
Elk v. Wilkins holds that Native Americans who had left their nations were still not U.S. citizens.
United States v. Wong Kim Ark applies birthright citizenship to a U.S.-born son of Chinese parents.
The Indian Citizenship Act makes Native Americans U.S. citizens.

misconception.myth: By making women citizens, the Fourteenth Amendment gave them the right to vote.
misconception.fact: Section 2 penalized states only for denying the vote to male citizens, and in Minor v. Happersett (1875) the Supreme Court held that citizenship did not carry the right to vote; women won a constitutional guarantee only with the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920.
misconception.why: Assuming citizenship and voting rights always went together hides how long women, and Native Americans after the 1924 citizenship act, were citizens who could still be kept from the polls.

title: Frederick Douglass
summary: An abolitionist, orator, editor and public official (c. 1818–1895) who escaped slavery in Maryland in 1838 and became the most prominent Black American voice of the nineteenth century, campaigning against slavery, for Black citizenship and voting rights, and for women's rights.

review.question: Why did publishing his Narrative in 1845 put Douglass in danger, and how was that danger resolved?
review.answer: The book named the people and places of his enslavement, exposing him as a fugitive who could be seized; he toured Britain and Ireland, where supporters raised $711.66 to buy his freedom from Hugh Auld, so he returned to the United States legally free in 1847.

review.question: How did Douglass's view of the Constitution change, and why does it matter?
review.answer: He first held William Lloyd Garrison's view that the Constitution was a proslavery compact, but between about 1848 and 1852 came to read it as an antislavery document; that let him work through politics and the law against slavery and broke his alliance with Garrison.

review.question: Why did Douglass support the Fifteenth Amendment even though it did not enfranchise women?
review.answer: He backed women's suffrage, but argued in 1869 that for Black Americans in the former slave states the vote was a matter of life and death, so Black men's voting rights could not wait for a separate women's amendment.

timeline.event: Born Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey in Talbot County, Maryland, according to a later ledger notation; he himself believed he was born about 1817.
Sent to Baltimore to live with Hugh and Sophia Auld, where he begins learning to read.
Hired out to Edward Covey, a so-called slave breaker, and fights back against his beatings.
Escapes to New York disguised as a sailor, using a free Black sailor's papers and a ticket paid for by Anna Murray.
Marries Anna Murray in New York; the couple settles in New Bedford, Massachusetts, as the Douglasses.
Hired as a lecturer by the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society.
Publishes Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass and begins a lecture tour of Britain and Ireland.
Returns legally free after supporters pay Hugh Auld $711.66; launches the North Star in Rochester, New York.
Seconds Elizabeth Cady Stanton's suffrage resolution at the Seneca Falls women's rights convention.
Delivers "What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?" at Corinthian Hall, Rochester.
Meets President Lincoln to protest unequal pay and treatment of Black soldiers.
At the American Equal Rights Association meeting, argues that Black men's voting rights are a matter of life and death.
Appointed U.S. marshal for the District of Columbia by President Hayes.
Appointed U.S. minister resident and consul general to Haiti, serving until 1891.
Dies at Cedar Hill, his Washington home, after attending a meeting of the National Council of Women.

misconception.myth: Douglass was born on February 14, 1818, a birthday recorded at the time.
misconception.fact: No record gives the day. Douglass believed he was born about 1817; a ledger kept by his enslaver Aaron Anthony notes February 1818, possibly added later, and Douglass chose February 14 to celebrate.
misconception.why: Enslaved people were routinely denied knowledge of their own birthdays, and the uncertainty is itself evidence of what slavery took from them.

title: George Washington
summary: A Virginia planter, surveyor and soldier (1732–1799) who commanded the Continental Army in the American Revolutionary War, presided over the Constitutional Convention and served as the first president of the United States (1789–1797), setting many precedents of the office while enslaving hundreds of people at Mount Vernon.

review.question: Why did Washington's will free only 123 of the 317 enslaved people living at Mount Vernon in 1799?
review.answer: Only 123 belonged to him; 153 were "dower" slaves from the estate of Martha Washington's first husband, which neither spouse could legally free and which passed to the Custis grandchildren, and 40 more were rented from a neighbor.

review.question: How did the Western Confederacy's victory over Arthur St. Clair in 1791 change Washington's frontier policy?
review.answer: After more than 630 of St. Clair's roughly 930 soldiers were killed, Washington and Congress built a larger, professionally trained Legion of the United States under Anthony Wayne, which won at Fallen Timbers in 1794 and forced the 1795 Treaty of Greenville cessions.

review.question: Why do historians disagree about whether Washington stood above party politics?
review.answer: He warned in his Farewell Address against the spirit of party and never joined a party, yet he sided with Hamilton against Jefferson and, in Encyclopedia Virginia's account, led a Federalist faction that voters rejected in 1800.

timeline.event: Born at Popes Creek in Westmoreland County, Virginia (February 11 under the Julian calendar then in use).
Surrenders Fort Necessity to French forces, a clash that helped open the Seven Years' War.
Takes his seat in the Virginia House of Burgesses, weeks after marrying Martha Dandridge Custis.
The Second Continental Congress appoints him commander in chief of the new Continental Army.
Crosses the Delaware on Christmas night and wins at Trenton, then at Princeton days later.
Lord Cornwallis surrenders the British army at Yorktown, Virginia.
Resigns his commission to Congress at Annapolis, Maryland.
Elected president of the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia.
Takes the oath as the first president at Federal Hall in New York City.
Western Confederacy warriors led by Little Turtle rout Arthur St. Clair's army on the Wabash.
Issues a proclamation of neutrality in the war between France and Britain.
His Farewell Address appears in a Philadelphia newspaper.
Leaves office after two terms.
Dies at Mount Vernon of an acute throat infection.
The 123 people Washington enslaved become free under his will, after Martha Washington signs a deed of manumission.

misconception.myth: George Washington wore wooden false teeth.
misconception.fact: Mount Vernon finds no wood in any of his dentures; they were made of human teeth, ivory, metal and probably cow and horse teeth, and staining could make them look like wood.
misconception.why: The myth hides a harder story, since some of the human teeth available to him may have come from enslaved people at Mount Vernon.

title: Great Railroad Strike of 1877
summary: A wave of strikes, protests and riots that began on the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad at Martinsburg, West Virginia, on July 16, 1877, spread along the rail lines from Baltimore to Chicago and St. Louis, and was put down by state militias and federal troops, leaving about a hundred people dead.

review.question: Why did a wage cut on one railroad turn into a crisis that stretched from Baltimore to St. Louis?
review.answer: Railroad workers had already suffered years of depression and repeated wage cuts since 1873, so when the Baltimore and Ohio announced another ten percent cut, the walkout at Martinsburg spread along the connected trunk lines, drew in unemployed people and workers in other trades, and local police and militias could not or would not stop it.

review.question: How did the federal government become involved, and what limits did President Hayes set on that role?
review.answer: Governors who said they could not keep order formally asked for federal help, and Hayes issued proclamations and sent Army troops; he refused the Pennsylvania Railroad's request to act directly for the companies and did not use soldiers to run trains, describing his aim as restoring order, though the deployment set a precedent for later presidents.

review.question: What lessons did workers and employers each draw from the strike?
review.answer: Many workers concluded they needed lasting, organized unions, while businesses concluded they needed more political influence and government help, including better-prepared state forces to deal with future labor unrest.

timeline.event: The railroads' financial bubble bursts, beginning years of depression, layoffs and repeated wage cuts.
Railroad workers at Martinsburg, West Virginia, walk off the job over a ten percent wage cut on the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad and stop trains.
Governor Henry M. Mathews asks for federal help, and President Rutherford B. Hayes proclaims that those obstructing the railroad must disperse by noon the next day.
Federal troops arrive at Martinsburg and end the violence there.
Hayes issues a similar proclamation for Maryland; in Pittsburgh, militia from Philadelphia fire into a crowd near the 28th Street crossing, killing about twenty people.
Fires in Pittsburgh destroy the Pennsylvania Railroad's Union Depot, more than thirty buildings and thousands of locomotives and cars.
Unrest in Chicago peaks over five days of walkouts, sympathy strikes and clashes with police, militia and U.S. Army troops.
By the end of July the strikes have largely been put down along the trunk lines.
By early 1880 the railroads have restored the wages they had cut.

misconception.myth: The 1877 strike was a planned national uprising, organized and directed by labor unions or radical leaders.
misconception.fact: The walkout began on the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad and spread largely on its own along the rail lines; almost none of the strikers belonged to a union and no leaders or organization controlled the strike as a whole, although local groups such as a railroad firemen's organization in West Virginia and socialists in Chicago and St. Louis played real roles in particular places.
misconception.why: The strike's sudden national reach and the visible part socialists played in a few cities made it look coordinated, and treating it as a conspiracy obscures the wage cuts and hard times that drove ordinary workers and their neighbours into the streets.

title: Indian Removal Act
summary: The federal law signed by President Andrew Jackson on May 28, 1830, that authorized the president to exchange lands west of the Mississippi River for the homelands of Native nations in the East, and that became the legal basis for the forced removal of the Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Choctaw, Chickasaw, Seminole and other nations in the 1830s and 1840s.

review.question: If the Indian Removal Act was written as a voluntary exchange of lands, how did it lead to the forced removal of the Cherokee Nation?
review.answer: The act let the president negotiate exchange treaties. When the Cherokee government under John Ross refused, federal agents concluded the Treaty of New Echota with a minority Treaty Party that had no authority to sign it; the Senate ratified it by a single vote, and in 1838 President Van Buren sent the army to round Cherokees into stockades and march them west.

review.question: Why did the Supreme Court's ruling in Worcester v. Georgia fail to stop removal?
review.answer: The Court held that Georgia's laws had no force in Cherokee territory, but neither Georgia nor President Jackson enforced the decision, so state pressure on Cherokee land continued.

review.question: Why do estimates of how many people were removed range from about 50,000 to about 88,000?
review.answer: The figures count different things — about 50,000 eastern Native people removed under Jackson's treaties, about 70,000 from the five southeastern nations over several decades, and about 88,000 including northern nations removed in the 1830s and 1840s.

timeline.event: Georgia cedes its western lands to the federal government, which promises in return to extinguish Indian land title within the state (the Compact of 1802).
After Andrew Jackson's forces defeat the Creeks at Horseshoe Bend, the Creeks surrender more than twenty million acres.
The Cherokee Nation adopts a written constitution; Georgia begins extending state jurisdiction over Cherokee territory.
Gold is found on Native lands in Georgia.
After passing the Senate 28 to 19 and the House 102 to 97, the Indian Removal Act is signed by President Jackson.
Jackson tells Congress that removal is nearing a 'happy consummation' and that two nations have agreed to terms.
The Supreme Court in Cherokee Nation v. Georgia calls the Cherokees a 'domestic dependent nation' and declines to hear their suit; Choctaw removal begins.
In Worcester v. Georgia the Court rules that Georgia's laws have no force in Cherokee territory; Georgia and the president do not enforce the ruling.
A minority Treaty Party signs the Treaty of New Echota without the authority of Principal Chief John Ross or the Cherokee government; the Second Seminole War begins the same year.
The Senate ratifies the New Echota treaty 31 to 15; most Muscogee (Creek) people are forced west.
Under orders from President Martin Van Buren, the army begins rounding up Cherokees into stockades.
The last Cherokee detachments reach Indian Territory, in present-day Oklahoma.
The reunited Cherokee Nation adopts a new constitution with its capital at Tahlequah.

misconception.myth: The Indian Removal Act itself ordered the army to drive Native nations out of the East.
misconception.fact: The act authorized the president to offer western lands in exchange for eastern homelands to nations that chose to make the exchange, and appropriated $500,000; the force came afterwards, through treaties obtained under heavy pressure — the Cherokee treaty was signed by a faction without the authority of the nation's government — and through troops sent to enforce them.
misconception.why: Knowing that the law was framed as voluntary exchange shows how coercion operated through treaties, state laws and enforcement decisions, and why the Cherokee and others fought removal in the courts and in Congress rather than simply in the field.

title: Japanese American incarceration during World War II
summary: The forced removal of people of Japanese ancestry from the U.S. West Coast under Executive Order 9066 and their imprisonment, without charges or trial, in War Relocation Authority camps and other sites from 1942 to 1946; about two-thirds of those held were U.S. citizens.

review.question: Why do the National Park Service and many historians prefer "incarceration" and "forced removal" to "internment" and "evacuation"?
review.answer: Internment is a law-of-war term for detaining enemy nationals, which the Justice Department and Army did separately to non-citizens; most people in the ten WRA camps were U.S. citizens held without charges, and "evacuation" wrongly suggests being moved out of danger.

review.question: How did the government justify the removal, and what does the evidence show?
review.answer: General DeWitt and President Roosevelt claimed military necessity, citing reports of signals and sabotage; those reports were unverified, the FBI's director mocked the Army's intelligence as hysterical, and no Japanese American was convicted of serious espionage or sabotage.

review.question: How did the Supreme Court's two December 1944 decisions differ?
review.answer: In Korematsu it upheld the exclusion order 6–3 as a military necessity, while in Ex parte Endo it ruled that the government could not keep detaining citizens it conceded were loyal; the exclusion orders were lifted effective January 2, 1945.

review.question: What did the redress movement achieve, and how?
review.answer: Japanese American organizations pressed Congress, which created a commission in 1980; its findings and recommendations led to the Civil Liberties Act of 1988, which apologized, paid $20,000 to each surviving incarcerated person (82,219 people in all) and funded public education.

timeline.event: Japan attacks Pearl Harbor; a presidential proclamation makes Japanese nationals in the U.S. liable to be detained as enemy aliens.
President Franklin D. Roosevelt signs Executive Order 9066, letting military commanders designate areas from which any person may be excluded.
Executive Order 9102 creates the War Relocation Authority (WRA) to run the camps.
Public Law 503 makes violating an exclusion order a federal crime.
The first Civilian Exclusion Order removes Japanese Americans from Bainbridge Island, Washington.
The Army activates the 442nd Regimental Combat Team, combining the 100th Battalion with mainland Nisei volunteers.
The WRA begins giving incarcerated adults the so-called loyalty questionnaire.
Tule Lake is designated a segregation center for people the government labeled disloyal.
The Supreme Court upholds exclusion in Korematsu v. United States but rules in Ex parte Endo that loyal citizens cannot be held.
The West Coast exclusion orders are lifted.
Tule Lake closes, the last of the ten WRA camps; the WRA is disbanded on June 30, 1946.
A federal court in San Francisco vacates Fred Korematsu's conviction, citing government misconduct.
President Ronald Reagan signs the Civil Liberties Act of 1988, with an apology and $20,000 for each surviving incarcerated person.

misconception.myth: Japanese Americans were removed and imprisoned because they were caught spying or committing sabotage, so the camps were a military necessity.
misconception.fact: No Japanese American was convicted of serious espionage or sabotage during the war; the rumours cited by the Army were unverified, and Congress later found the policy was driven by racial prejudice, war hysteria and a failure of political leadership.
misconception.why: The government justified the removal as military necessity at the time, the Supreme Court accepted that claim in 1944, and the word "evacuation" made forced removal sound like protection.

title: Jazz
summary: A form of music created by African American musicians in New Orleans around the turn of the twentieth century, blending blues, ragtime, brass-band and dance traditions with collective and solo improvisation, which spread across the United States and the world through recordings, migration and touring.

review.question: How did the segregation laws of the 1890s help shape early jazz in New Orleans?
review.answer: They stripped Creoles of color of their separate social status and pushed them together with uptown Black musicians, combining the Creoles' formal training and discipline with the improvised, blues-based playing of uptown bands.

review.question: Why is the story that jazz musicians left New Orleans because Storyville closed misleading?
review.answer: Many musicians, such as Jelly Roll Morton, the Original Creole Orchestra and Tom Brown's band, had left before the district closed in November 1917, and research on musicians who left between 1902 and 1922 shows they sought better pay, working conditions, racial equality and safety; King Oliver, for example, had been repeatedly arrested while playing.

review.question: How did bebop change the role of jazz compared with the swing era?
review.answer: Swing big bands played largely for dancing, while bebop, developed in Harlem after-hours sessions in the early 1940s, used small groups, fast tempos and improvised solos over chord changes, and was meant mainly for listening.

timeline.event: New Orleans begins sanctioning Sunday ring shouts by enslaved and free Black people at Place Congo (Congo Square), a practice allowed until 1856.
Around this time uptown cornetist Charles "Buddy" Bolden begins improvising on the blues and speeding up dance tunes, a style many early musicians later called the first jazz.
Pianist and composer Jelly Roll Morton begins touring outside New Orleans.
Tom Brown's band leaves New Orleans for Chicago.
The Original Dixieland Jazz Band makes the first commercial jazz recordings in New York City.
New Orleans closes its Storyville red-light district.
Kid Ory's band records in California, the first recording by a Black New Orleans jazz band; Louis Armstrong joins King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band in Chicago.
Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings (1925–1928) begin shifting jazz toward the improvising soloist.
Duke Ellington's band begins its engagement at Harlem's whites-only Cotton Club, with nightly radio broadcasts.
Thelonious Monk is house pianist at Minton's Playhouse in Harlem, where after-hours sessions help create bebop.
Dizzy Gillespie makes the first major-label bebop recording, for RCA's Bluebird label.
The State Department sends Dizzy Gillespie on the first of its Cold War jazz-ambassador tours.

misconception.myth: Jazz was born in the brothels of Storyville, and its musicians scattered north when the district was closed in 1917.
misconception.fact: Jazz grew out of New Orleans neighborhood life — brass bands, parades, dance halls, social clubs and street music — and Storyville was only one of many places musicians worked. Research by Tulane's Hogan Jazz Archive curator Bruce Raeburn on musicians who left the city between 1902 and 1922 found that they went for better pay, working conditions, racial equality and safety, not because the district closed; several had left years before 1917.
misconception.why: The red-light story is colorful and easy to tell, but it hides the African American and Creole communities, institutions and traditions that actually produced the music, and the segregation and police harassment that drove many musicians away.

title: Jim Crow laws
summary: The state and local laws, backed by custom and violence, that enforced racial segregation and stripped Black Americans of voting rights, mainly in the South and border states, from the end of Reconstruction until federal laws and court rulings dismantled them in the 1950s and 1960s.

review.question: Why did historians argue for decades about when Jim Crow began?
review.answer: C. Vann Woodward held that legal segregation was not inevitable and arrived mainly in the 1890s after a more fluid period, while critics such as Joel Williamson and Howard Rabinowitz found segregation by custom, and in some places by law, already in place during Reconstruction; the dispute shapes whether Jim Crow is seen as a legacy of slavery or a new system built by later choices.

review.question: How did southern states keep Black citizens from voting despite the Fifteenth Amendment?
review.answer: They used poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses, white primaries and new state constitutions such as Louisiana's of 1898 and Alabama's of 1901, enforced alongside economic intimidation and violence including lynching.

review.question: Which federal actions dismantled the Jim Crow system?
review.answer: Court rulings such as Brown v. Board of Education (1954), Harper v. Virginia State Board of Elections (1966) and Loving v. Virginia (1967), together with the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act of 1965 and the Civil Rights Act of 1968.

timeline.event: Thomas Dartmouth Rice first performs the blackface minstrel routine "Jump Jim Crow," source of the later name for segregation.
Alabama adopts a Black Code controlling the labor and movement of freed people.
Tennessee's Chapter 130 permits discrimination in hotels, theaters, trains and streetcars.
Tennessee orders segregated railroad cars, a law often called the first Jim Crow law.
In the Civil Rights Cases the Supreme Court strikes down key parts of the Civil Rights Act of 1875.
Louisiana passes the Separate Car Act, one of nine state laws of 1887–1892 separating passengers by race.
Plessy v. Ferguson upholds state-mandated segregation under the separate but equal doctrine.
Louisiana's new constitution mandates segregated schools and restricts Black men's voting.
Alabama's constitution disfranchises Black voters, segregates schools and bars interracial marriage.
In Guinn v. United States the Supreme Court rules Oklahoma's grandfather clause violates the Fifteenth Amendment.
Brown v. Board of Education declares school segregation unconstitutional.
The Civil Rights Act outlaws segregation in businesses such as theaters, restaurants and hotels.
President Johnson signs the Voting Rights Act.
Harper v. Virginia State Board of Elections holds Virginia's poll tax unconstitutional.
Loving v. Virginia unanimously strikes down a state ban on interracial marriage.
A new Civil Rights Act prohibits discrimination in housing.

misconception.myth: Jim Crow laws existed only in the former Confederate states.
misconception.fact: Most Jim Crow laws were passed in the South, but border states adopted them too, Oklahoma used a grandfather clause to bar Black voters until 1915, and Black Northerners met segregation in schools and public accommodations.
misconception.why: Treating segregation as a purely regional custom hides how widely racial discrimination operated and why the civil rights movement sought national laws to end it.

title: Louisiana Purchase
summary: The 1803 agreement in which the United States paid France $15 million for its claim to Louisiana, about 828,000 square miles west of the Mississippi River, roughly doubling the nation's size while leaving the land itself in the hands of the Native nations who lived there.

review.question: Why did Jefferson's envoys end up buying far more land than they were sent to get?
review.answer: They were authorized to pay up to $10 million for New Orleans and the Floridas, but Napoleon, whose army had been devastated in Saint-Domingue and who faced renewed war with Britain, offered all of Louisiana, so Livingston and Monroe exceeded their instructions and agreed to $15 million for the whole territory.

review.question: How did the purchase test Jefferson's own view of the Constitution, and how did he resolve it?
review.answer: Jefferson believed the Constitution made no provision for acquiring foreign territory and drafted an amendment, but his Cabinet argued it was unnecessary and Napoleon's deadline loomed, so he let the Senate ratify the treaty without one, comparing himself to a guardian investing a ward's money in adjacent land.

review.question: According to Robert Lee, what did the United States actually acquire from France, and why does that change the meaning of the $15 million price?
review.answer: It acquired France's claim of preemption — the exclusive right to obtain land from Native nations — rather than the land itself, so the real cost of the territory was paid later through many treaties and cessions backed by force, adding up to far more than $15 million.

timeline.event: A treaty with Spain (Pinckney's Treaty) lets Americans navigate the Mississippi and deposit goods at New Orleans for export.
France reacquires Louisiana from Spain.
Spain's King Charles IV signs the decree transferring Louisiana to France, and the Spanish official at New Orleans revokes Americans' right of deposit.
Jefferson sends James Monroe as minister extraordinary to join Robert Livingston in Paris, authorized to pay up to $10 million for New Orleans and the Floridas.
French foreign minister Talleyrand tells Livingston that France will sell all of Louisiana.
Livingston, Monroe and François Barbé-Marbois sign the treaty of cession and two financial conventions in Paris.
The purchase is officially announced in the United States.
The Senate ratifies the treaty by a vote of 24 to 7.
Spain formally returns Louisiana to France.
France transfers Louisiana to the United States at New Orleans.
Congress creates the Territory of Orleans from the southern part of the purchase.
More than eighty enslaved people launch the German Coast uprising upriver from New Orleans.
Louisiana is admitted as a state; President James Madison signs the statehood law.
The Adams-Onís (Transcontinental) Treaty with Spain finally settles the purchase's disputed borders.

misconception.myth: In 1803 the United States bought the land of the Louisiana Territory from France for a few cents an acre.
misconception.fact: France sold what it had, a European claim to sovereignty that gave the United States the exclusive right to acquire land from the Native nations who held and lived on it; the United States then acquired that land over the following decades through hundreds of treaties, agreements and seizures, eventually paying Native nations about $2.6 billion in disbursements by one historian's count.
misconception.why: The famous price makes the purchase look like a single real-estate bargain and erases the Native nations whose lands were the real subject of later negotiation, pressure and war.

title: Mississippi River
summary: North America's second-longest river, flowing about 2,340 miles from Lake Itasca in Minnesota to the Gulf of Mexico and draining roughly 1.2 million square miles of the interior; a homeland and highway for Native nations, a prize of empires and the Civil War, and a heavily engineered shipping and flood-control system today.

review.question: Why is it inaccurate to call the Mississippi the longest river in the United States, and why do published lengths for it differ?
review.answer: The Missouri, which flows into it, is longer (2,540 miles against 2,340 in the USGS list, or about 100 miles longer by the Park Service's count); figures for the Mississippi itself range from about 2,300 to 2,350 miles because agencies measure a shifting channel differently.

review.question: Why did Union leaders consider capturing Vicksburg essential?
review.answer: The Confederacy had closed the Mississippi to Northern commerce; taking Vicksburg would reopen the river to Midwestern farm exports, split the South in two and cut a vital Confederate supply line.

review.question: How did the Great Flood of 1927 change federal flood-control policy, and who bore its heaviest costs?
review.answer: It showed that levees alone could not hold the river, so the 1928 Flood Control Act added spillways, floodways and diversion works; the heaviest costs fell on displaced residents, including many Black tenant farmers who were segregated in relief shelters and later left for northern cities.

timeline.event: The Mississippian culture flourishes in the river valley; its greatest center, Cahokia, rises near present-day St. Louis and lasts until about 1350.
Spanish explorer Hernando de Soto becomes one of the first Europeans to travel the river.
Louis Jolliet and the Jesuit Jacques Marquette travel the river for France.
Pinckney's Treaty with Spain opens the river to American ships and duty-free transport through New Orleans.
Confederate forces surrender Vicksburg, Mississippi, ending a campaign for control of the river.
During the Great Flood of 1927, engineers begin dynamiting the levee at Caernarvon, Louisiana, below New Orleans.
Congress passes the Flood Control Act, shifting federal policy from levees alone to spillways and floodways.
A major summer flood strikes the upper river basin.

misconception.myth: The Mississippi is the longest river in the United States.
misconception.fact: The U.S. Geological Survey lists the Missouri River, the Mississippi's largest tributary, at 2,540 miles against the Mississippi's 2,340, and the National Park Service also describes the Missouri as about 100 miles longer.
misconception.why: The Mississippi carries the larger flow and the larger name, and the two rivers are often added together as one system, so its length record gets assumed rather than checked.

title: Morrill Land-Grant College Act
summary: The federal law signed by President Abraham Lincoln on July 2, 1862, that gave each loyal state 30,000 acres of federal land or land scrip per member of Congress to endow colleges teaching agriculture and the mechanic arts, founding the land-grant university system — largely with land taken from Native nations.

review.question: Why could the Morrill Act pass in 1862 when a similar bill had failed in 1859?
review.answer: President Buchanan vetoed the 1859 bill on fiscal and constitutional grounds; after Southern states seceded, Morrill reintroduced it with added emphasis on military instruction and Lincoln signed it on July 2, 1862.

review.question: How did a law about colleges in the East depend on Native land in the West?
review.answer: States without enough federal land received scrip to claim and sell Western land, and Western states selected land within their borders; researchers traced about 10.7 million acres to cessions from nearly 250 tribes, bands and communities, for which the United States paid less than $400,000, often nothing.

review.question: How did the 1890 Morrill Act reshape the system the 1862 act began?
review.answer: It added annual federal funding and barred racial discrimination in admissions, but let states meet that rule with separate institutions "of like character," which produced the 19 historically Black 1890 Institutions in the segregated South.

timeline.event: Illinois College professor Jonathan Baldwin Turner proposes state industrial universities at a farmers' convention in Putnam County, Illinois.
Representative Justin Smith Morrill of Vermont introduces a national land-grant college bill.
President James Buchanan vetoes the bill passed by Congress, citing cost and constitutional limits on federal power.
Morrill reintroduces the bill after Southern states secede.
Lincoln signs the Morrill Act; states in rebellion are excluded from its grants.
The Hatch Act funds agricultural experiment stations at the land-grant colleges.
A second Morrill Act adds annual appropriations and leads to the founding of separate land-grant institutions for Black students in the segregated South.
The Smith-Lever Act creates the Cooperative Extension System.
The Equity in Educational Land-Grant Status Act makes tribal colleges and universities land-grant institutions.

misconception.myth: Land-grant universities are so called because the federal government gave them the land their campuses stand on.
misconception.fact: The act gave states land or scrip — vouchers for distant federal land — to sell; the proceeds became a permanent endowment that could not be spent on buildings, and most of that land had been taken from Native nations through cessions, many of them coerced.
misconception.why: The campus story hides where the money came from — New York's scrip, sold to fund Cornell, and Dakota land ceded in Minnesota endowed colleges far from the land itself.

title: New Orleans
summary: Louisiana's largest city, founded by the French in 1718 on a natural levee near the mouth of the Mississippi River on land Choctaw speakers call Bulbancha; a colonial capital, the nation's largest antebellum slave market, the birthplace of jazz, and a low-lying port whose levees failed during Hurricane Katrina in 2005.

review.question: Why did the French choose the site of New Orleans, and what Indigenous knowledge shaped that choice?
review.answer: Bienville was told to build a city near the Mississippi's mouth to keep British and Spanish rivals from moving up the river; Native people had told his brother Iberville's 1699 expedition of a ridge (now Esplanade Ridge) linking the river to Bayou St. John and Lake Pontchartrain, which made the spot strategically valuable.

review.question: Why did Jefferson want New Orleans, and how did that lead to the Louisiana Purchase?
review.answer: Its port was the outlet for produce from more than a third of the country, and Spain's refusal in 1802 to let Americans deposit goods there angered westerners; Jefferson told Livingston to buy the city, and the negotiations ended in the April 30, 1803 treaty for all of Louisiana.

review.question: How did events in New Orleans shape Reconstruction and the fight against segregation?
review.answer: The 1866 Mechanics' Institute massacre helped bring about Radical Reconstruction and stronger congressional action, including the Fourteenth Amendment's citizenship guarantees; in 1891 the city's Comité des Citoyens organized and funded the legal challenge to the Separate Car Law that became Plessy v. Ferguson.

review.question: Why did so much of the city flood in 2005 when its oldest districts stayed relatively high?
review.answer: Most of the city was built on drained swamp that has subsided since the early 1900s, creating a bowl below sea level; when levees separating the city from Lake Pontchartrain broke during Katrina, at least 80 percent of New Orleans flooded, while the original city on natural levees stood 5 to 10 feet above sea level.

timeline.event: Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville's French expedition learns from Native guides of a ridge linking the Mississippi to Bayou St. John and Lake Pontchartrain.
Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville founds La Nouvelle-Orléans near the river's mouth.
France makes New Orleans the capital of French Louisiana.
The U.S. flag is raised in New Orleans as Louisiana passes to the United States.
Andrew Jackson's forces defeat a British army below the city, after the Treaty of Ghent was signed but before it took effect.
The city's enslaved population peaks at 23,448, nearly a quarter of its residents.
White mobs, joined by police, kill nearly fifty people at the Mechanics' Institute during a convention seeking Black men's voting rights.
Creole of color activists announce the Comité des Citoyens to challenge Louisiana's Separate Car Law.
Cornetist Buddy Bolden forms his own band, an early landmark of New Orleans jazz.
After levee breaches during Hurricane Katrina, at least 80 percent of the city lies under floodwater.
The 2020 census counts 383,997 residents.

misconception.myth: All of New Orleans lies below sea level.
misconception.fact: A 2005 USGS statement to Congress put more than half of the city below sea level, some areas by as much as 10 feet, while the original city sat on natural river levees about 5 to 10 feet above sea level, and those old levees and sandy ridges remain above it.
misconception.why: Katrina's floodwaters covering most of the city made the "bowl" image memorable, but the oldest neighborhoods stand on the high ground the founders chose, and the low areas are largely drained swamp that has sunk since the early 1900s.

title: Panic of 1873
summary: A financial crisis that began when the railroad-financing bank Jay Cooke and Company failed on September 18, 1873, closed the New York Stock Exchange for ten days, and set off a depression that lasted until about 1879, ruining thousands of businesses, sinking the Freedman's Savings Bank and helping to turn national politics away from Reconstruction.

review.question: How did a stock market crash in Europe help cause a banking panic in the United States?
review.answer: After the Vienna crashes of 1873, European investors sold American securities, especially railroad bonds; that cut off the borrowing that overbuilt railroads depended on, many defaulted on their bank loans, and when Jay Cooke and Company, deeply invested in the Northern Pacific Railway, failed on September 18, depositors rushed to withdraw their money from banks across the country.

review.question: Why did the panic fall so hard on Black depositors of the Freedman's Savings Bank?
review.answer: After an 1870 charter change, the bank's trustees had put depositors' savings into railroads, real estate and risky loans; the panic made most of those investments worthless, runs drained its cash, and when it closed in June 1874 its deposits had no federal protection, so only about half of the depositors ever received anything, and they recovered roughly three-fifths of their balances.

review.question: Why do historians link the depression that followed the panic to the end of Reconstruction?
review.answer: The downturn pushed economic issues ahead of Reconstruction on the national agenda, eroded Northern willingness to keep intervening in the South, and helped Democrats win the House in 1874, while white Southern Democrats were regaining power state by state; historians differ on how much weight to give the economy versus Southern political violence.

timeline.event: A stock market crash in Vienna, Austria, the first of two that year, leads European investors to start selling American securities, especially railroad bonds.
Jay Cooke and Company, heavily invested in the Northern Pacific Railway, suspends payments and goes bankrupt.
The New York Stock Exchange closes for the first time in its history and stays shut for ten days.
The New York Clearing House suspends cash payments in New York.
The acute panic subsides by mid-October, but a long depression follows.
Frederick Douglass is elected president of the struggling Freedman's Savings and Trust Company; Congress passes a bill to issue more greenback currency, which President Grant vetoes.
The Freedman's Savings and Trust Company closes, days after Congress puts its assets under a three-member board.
The Specie Resumption Act commits the Treasury to retire greenbacks and return to gold-backed currency within four years.
Railroad wage cuts during the depression set off the Great Railroad Strike.
The depression begins to lift early in the year.

misconception.myth: The Panic of 1873 was a purely American crash that began on Wall Street when Jay Cooke's bank failed.
misconception.fact: Cooke's failure turned the strain into a U.S. panic, but stock market crashes in Vienna in May and September 1873 had already led European investors to dump American railroad bonds, cutting off the credit that overbuilt U.S. railroads needed.
misconception.why: Seeing the transatlantic origins shows how closely American railroads and banks already depended on European capital, and why a crash abroad could ruin firms, workers and depositors across the United States.

title: Plessy v. Ferguson
summary: The 1896 U.S. Supreme Court decision that upheld a Louisiana law requiring separate railroad cars for Black and white passengers, giving constitutional approval to state-imposed racial segregation under what became known as the "separate but equal" doctrine.

review.question: Why did Homer Plessy board a whites-only car on a train that stayed inside Louisiana rather than an interstate train?
review.answer: Weeks earlier, in Abbott v. Hicks, the Louisiana Supreme Court had ruled that the Separate Car Act did not apply to interstate passengers, so the Comité des Citoyens needed an intrastate trip to test the law's constitutionality directly.

review.question: How did Justice Brown's majority answer the argument that forced separation stamped Black citizens as inferior?
review.answer: He said any such stigma did not come from the law itself but from how Black Americans chose to interpret it, and he treated segregation as a reasonable use of a state's police power that could take established customs into account.

review.question: Why is Plessy considered so consequential even though it concerned railroad cars?
review.answer: By holding that state-mandated separation did not violate the Fourteenth Amendment if accommodations were nominally equal, it gave legal cover to segregation in schools, transportation and public life for more than half a century, until Brown v. Board of Education rejected the doctrine in public education in 1954.

timeline.event: Louisiana's legislature passes the Separate Car Act (Act No. 111), requiring separate railroad cars for Black and white passengers.
Eighteen New Orleans residents form the Comité des Citoyens to challenge the law in court.
Daniel Desdunes boards a whites-only car on an interstate train in a first test case.
In Abbott v. Hicks the Louisiana Supreme Court rules that the act does not apply to interstate passengers.
Homer Plessy is arrested after sitting in the whites-only coach of an East Louisiana Railroad train to Covington.
Judge John Howard Ferguson of the Orleans Parish Criminal Court rules against Plessy.
The Louisiana Supreme Court upholds Ferguson's ruling.
The U.S. Supreme Court affirms, 7 to 1, with Justice Henry Billings Brown writing and Justice John Marshall Harlan dissenting.
Plessy pleads guilty in New Orleans and pays a $25 fine.
Brown v. Board of Education rejects separate but equal in public education.
Louisiana Governor John Bel Edwards grants Plessy a posthumous pardon.

misconception.myth: The Supreme Court's majority opinion in Plessy announced the phrase "separate but equal."
misconception.fact: The majority opinion speaks of the statute's "equal but separate" accommodations; the words "separate but equal" appear in Justice Harlan's dissent, and the label for the doctrine became common afterward.
misconception.why: Knowing the exact wording shows that the Court was approving a state statute's own formula, and that the promise of equality was a legislative claim the majority accepted rather than tested.

title: September 11 attacks
summary: The coordinated al Qaeda terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, in which 19 hijackers seized four U.S. airliners and crashed them into the World Trade Center in New York City, the Pentagon in Virginia and a field in Somerset County, Pennsylvania, killing nearly 3,000 people.

review.question: Why did the 9/11 Commission call imagination the most important failure before the attacks?
review.answer: Officials had warnings about al Qaeda and earlier attacks such as the 1998 embassy bombings and the 2000 USS Cole attack, but no one treated the use of hijacked airliners as weapons as a real threat; the Commission found that U.S. measures between 1998 and 2001 never disturbed or delayed the plot.

review.question: How did the actions of the people aboard United 93 change the outcome of the attacks?
review.answer: After learning by phone of the other hijackings, the passengers and crew voted to fight back and forced the plane down in a Pennsylvania field about 20 minutes' flying time from Washington, so it never reached its probable target, the U.S. Capitol or the White House.

review.question: How did the attacks reshape the federal government at home?
review.answer: Within weeks the president created a White House Office of Homeland Security, Congress passed the USA PATRIOT Act and created the TSA in 2001, and the Homeland Security Act of 2002 merged 22 agencies into a new Cabinet department; the 9/11 Commission's 2004 report then led to proposals such as a National Counterterrorism Center and a national intelligence director.

timeline.event: Al Qaeda leader Usama Bin Ladin approves the airliner plot conceived by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed (late 1998 or early 1999).
By early July all 19 hijackers, who had begun entering the country in January 2000, are inside the United States.

Hijacked airliners strike the World Trade Center's North Tower (8:46 a.m.) and South Tower (9:03 a.m.) and the Pentagon (9:37 a.m.); United 93 crashes in Pennsylvania at 10:03 a.m. after a passenger and crew revolt.
President George W. Bush signs the Authorization for Use of Military Force against those responsible.
Bush signs the USA PATRIOT Act, expanding surveillance and security powers.
U.S. air strikes against Taliban and al Qaeda targets in Afghanistan begin Operation Enduring Freedom.
The recovery effort at Ground Zero formally ends with the removal of the Last Column.
The Department of Homeland Security opens, combining parts or all of 22 federal agencies.
The bipartisan 9/11 Commission issues its final report and closes on August 21, 2004.
NIST issues its final report on the collapse of the Twin Towers.
The National September 11 Memorial opens to the public, a day after its dedication on the tenth anniversary.

misconception.myth: The Twin Towers were brought down by a planned controlled demolition using explosives or thermite rather than by the hijacked planes.
misconception.fact: The federal engineering investigation by NIST found that the impacts severed columns and stripped fireproofing, and that multi-floor fires weakened floors that pulled the perimeter columns inward until they failed; it found no corroborating evidence for explosives, and seismic signals came from falling debris after each collapse began.
misconception.why: The towers' sudden, total collapse was unprecedented and hard to grasp, and demolition stories replace a documented chain of failures and warnings with a hidden plot that the engineering and investigative record does not support.

title: Siege of Vicksburg
summary: The 47-day Union siege of the Confederate river fortress at Vicksburg, Mississippi, from May 18 to July 4, 1863, in which Ulysses S. Grant's army forced John C. Pemberton's garrison to surrender, giving the Union control of the Mississippi River and splitting the Confederacy.

review.question: Why did both sides consider Vicksburg so important?
review.answer: Confederate guns on its bluffs blocked Union traffic on the Mississippi, on which Midwestern farmers depended, and the city linked the eastern Confederacy to the supplies and men of Louisiana, Arkansas and Texas; taking it would reopen the river and split the South.

review.question: How did Grant finally get his army into position to besiege Vicksburg after months of failure?
review.answer: He crossed the river south of the city on April 30–May 1, 1863, won a string of battles inland through May 17 that drove Pemberton back into the city, and after two failed assaults on May 19 and 22 settled into a siege.

review.question: Why did Pemberton surrender on July 4 rather than fight his way out?
review.answer: After about six weeks of siege, hunger and disease had worn down his garrison; his commanders judged a breakout impossible, and Grant's offer to parole the men rather than imprison them was the best term available.

review.question: How did the fall of Vicksburg lead to Union control of the entire Mississippi?
review.answer: The garrison at Port Hudson, Louisiana, the last Confederate stronghold on the river, surrendered on July 9, 1863, after learning Vicksburg had fallen, opening the river from its source to New Orleans.
