timeline.event: Union gunboats attack Vicksburg from upriver in the spring but eventually withdraw; Grant's first overland and river attempts follow that fall.
Grant's army crosses the Mississippi from Louisiana into Mississippi south of Vicksburg on the night of April 30–May 1.
Union victory at Port Gibson opens an inland campaign that wins at Raymond, Jackson, Champion Hill and the Big Black River by May 17.
Grant's Army of the Tennessee reaches the Confederate defenses of Vicksburg.
Sherman's corps assaults the Stockade Redan and is repulsed with about 1,000 Union casualties.
A second general assault on a three-mile front fails, and Grant settles into a siege.
Black Union regiments help repel a Confederate attack on the supply post at Milliken's Bend, Louisiana.
Union engineers explode 2,200 pounds of black powder under a Confederate redan on the Jackson Road; the crater fight gains no ground.
Pemberton and Grant meet between the lines; that night Grant offers to parole the garrison.
At 10 a.m. some 29,000 Confederates march out, stack their arms and surrender the city.
Port Hudson, Louisiana, surrenders after learning of Vicksburg's fall, opening the whole Mississippi to Union navigation.
Lincoln's public letter to James C. Conkling celebrates the reopened river and credits Black soldiers.
The last Union occupation troops, including U.S. Colored Troops, are withdrawn from Vicksburg.
The Mississippi African-American Monument is dedicated in Vicksburg National Military Park.

misconception.myth: Lincoln's line that the Father of Waters again flowed "unvexed to the sea" was his spontaneous reaction to the news from Vicksburg.
misconception.fact: The sentence appears in a public letter he wrote to James C. Conkling on August 26, 1863, nearly two months after the surrender, in a passage that also credits soldiers from many regions and Black troops.
misconception.why: Detaching the line from the letter loses Lincoln's purpose, which was to defend emancipation and Black enlistment to Northern critics by pointing to victories like Vicksburg.

title: Slavery in the United States
aliases: Chattel slavery in the United States
summary: The system of hereditary, race-based chattel slavery that held people of African descent, and in the colonial era many Native Americans, as property in the English colonies and the United States from the early 1600s until the Thirteenth Amendment abolished it in 1865.

review.question: Why did Virginia's 1662 law matter so much for slavery's growth?
review.answer: It made a child's status follow the mother's rather than the father's, so every child of an enslaved woman was born enslaved; slavery became hereditary and could grow through births rather than only through imports.

review.question: How did the enslaved population grow from about 700,000 in 1790 to nearly 4 million in 1860 even though importing enslaved people was banned from 1808?
review.answer: Because children of enslaved mothers were born enslaved, the population grew through births, and the domestic slave trade then moved about a million people from the Upper South to the cotton-growing Deep South.

review.question: How did slavery reach into the free states before the Civil War?
review.answer: The Constitution's fugitive slave clause required people escaping bondage to be returned, and the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 used federal commissioners without juries to send about 1,000 Black Americans South, provoking resistance in northern communities.

timeline.event: The English privateer White Lion lands about twenty captive Africans at Point Comfort, Virginia, and sells them for food.
Virginia's General Assembly rules that a child is enslaved or free according to the mother's status, making slavery hereditary.
A Virginia law classes enslaved people as real estate.
Pennsylvania passes a gradual emancipation law.
The federal ban on importing enslaved people takes effect.
Slavery ends in New York under its 1817 law.
Nat Turner's rebellion begins in Southampton County, Virginia.
Congress passes a Fugitive Slave Act that denies accused people a jury trial.
The census counts 3,953,760 enslaved people, the peak and the last census to count them.
General Order No. 3 announces freedom in Galveston, Texas, the origin of Juneteenth.
The Thirteenth Amendment is ratified, abolishing slavery nationwide.
New Jersey's governor signs a state constitutional amendment ending slavery there.

misconception.myth: Slavery was a purely Southern institution that the North never practised.
misconception.fact: Slavery was legal in the North too; enslaved people were 30 percent of Kings County (Brooklyn) residents in 1790, New York's final emancipation came only in 1827, and about 16 people in New Jersey were still legally enslaved in December 1865.
misconception.why: Treating slavery as only Southern hides how gradual and incomplete northern emancipation was, and how northern banks and merchants profited from the cotton economy.

title: Thirteenth Amendment
aliases: Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution
summary: The 1865 amendment to the U.S. Constitution that abolished slavery and involuntary servitude throughout the United States, except as punishment for a crime, and gave Congress power to enforce that ban.

review.question: Why did Lincoln and Congress believe a constitutional amendment was needed even after the Emancipation Proclamation?
review.answer: The proclamation rested on Lincoln's war powers and applied only to areas in rebellion, not to loyal border states; its legal force after the war was doubtful, so an amendment was the only secure way to end slavery everywhere.

review.question: How did the 1864 election and the end of the war help the amendment pass and be ratified?
review.answer: After the House first failed to reach two-thirds, Lincoln's reelection campaign put the amendment on the Republican platform and a lame-duck session passed it in January 1865; later, President Andrew Johnson required Southern states seeking readmission to abolish slavery, and Georgia's ratification in December 1865 completed the three-fourths.

review.question: Why is the amendment's exception "as a punishment for crime" significant?
review.answer: Southern states used criminal convictions to lease mostly Black prisoners to private companies, as Georgia did from 1868 to 1908, and scholars still debate whether the framers meant the clause to permit that kind of forced labor.

timeline.event: Congress passes the Corwin Amendment, which would have shielded slavery in the states; it is never ratified.
The Emancipation Proclamation takes effect, but only in areas in rebellion.
The Senate Judiciary Committee under Lyman Trumbull reports the amendment to the full Senate.
The Senate passes the amendment, 38 to 6.
The House passes the amendment, 119 to 56, after earlier votes fell short.
Lincoln approves the joint resolution sending the amendment to the states.
Georgia becomes the 27th state to ratify, completing the three-fourths needed.
Secretary of State William H. Seward proclaims the amendment ratified.

misconception.myth: The Emancipation Proclamation ended slavery throughout the United States.
misconception.fact: The 1863 proclamation applied only to areas in rebellion and left slavery legal in loyal border states; slavery ended nationwide only with the Thirteenth Amendment, which freed people still enslaved in Delaware and Kentucky in December 1865.
misconception.why: Confusing a wartime executive order with a constitutional amendment hides why abolitionists, Congress and Lincoln fought for an amendment, and how close slavery came to surviving the war.

title: Thomas Jefferson
summary: A Virginia planter, lawyer and founder (1743–1826) who drafted the Declaration of Independence, wrote Virginia's statute for religious freedom, served as secretary of state and vice president, and was the third president of the United States (1801–1809), while holding more than 600 people in slavery over his lifetime.

review.question: Why did the House of Representatives, not the voters or the electors, decide the presidential election of 1800?
review.answer: Electors then cast two undifferentiated votes, so Jefferson and his running mate Aaron Burr tied at 73 electoral votes each; the Federalist-controlled House deadlocked for 35 ballots before choosing Jefferson on the 36th, on February 17, 1801.

review.question: How did the Louisiana Purchase test Jefferson's own reading of the Constitution?
review.answer: Jefferson doubted that the Constitution gave the president power to acquire territory and considered an amendment, but public support and the land's value led him to set aside his strict reading, a choice that helped build the principle of implied federal powers.

review.question: How did Jefferson's 1803 letter to William Henry Harrison propose to obtain Native land?
review.answer: He proposed government trading houses that would draw Native leaders into debt, which they would pay off by ceding land, and he expected Native nations either to be absorbed as citizens or to move west of the Mississippi.

timeline.event: Born at Shadwell plantation in western Virginia.
Admitted to the Virginia bar.
Enters the Virginia House of Burgesses, where he serves until 1774.
As a delegate to the Second Continental Congress, drafts the Declaration of Independence.
His wife, Martha Wayles Jefferson, dies after childbirth.
Begins about four years as American minister to France.
Virginia's General Assembly adopts his bill for religious freedom, first drafted in 1777.
Becomes secretary of state under George Washington; resigns in 1793.
Becomes vice president under John Adams after finishing second in the 1796 electoral vote.
The House of Representatives elects him president on its 36th ballot, breaking a 73-73 electoral tie with Aaron Burr.
The United States buys Louisiana from France for $15 million.
In a private letter to William Henry Harrison, lays out a plan to acquire Native lands through trade debts.
Signs the act banning the importation of enslaved people, effective January 1, 1808.
Congress passes his Embargo Act, barring American ships from leaving U.S. ports.
Signs the Non-Intercourse Act replacing the embargo, three days before leaving office.
Dies at Monticello, fifty years after the Declaration's approval.

misconception.myth: Thomas Jefferson wrote that the government is best which governs least.
misconception.fact: The Thomas Jefferson Foundation finds no such line in his writings; the earliest known printing of the wording is John L. O'Sullivan's 1837 introduction to the Democratic Review, and the earliest known attribution to Jefferson dates only from 1853.
misconception.why: The phrase was long associated with the political heirs of Jefferson's Democratic-Republican party, so it drifted onto the party's founder, and a familiar name makes a slogan sound authoritative.

title: United States Congress
summary: The legislative branch of the U.S. federal government, created by Article I of the Constitution: a two-chamber body made up of the House of Representatives, apportioned among the states by population, and the Senate, with two members per state, which first met in 1789.

review.question: Why does Congress have two chambers with different bases of representation?
review.answer: The framers created a bicameral legislature in July 1787 in which House seats are apportioned among the states by population while every state has two senators, balancing the interests of populous and small states.

review.question: How did the Seventeenth Amendment change the Senate, and why was it adopted?
review.answer: It replaced election of senators by state legislatures with election by the people; legislative selection had produced long deadlocks (45 in 20 states between 1891 and 1905), vacant seats and bribery cases, and many states had already moved to popular choice through primaries before the amendment was ratified in 1913.

review.question: How did the original Constitution's formula for apportioning House seats involve slavery?
review.answer: Article I counted the whole number of free persons, excluded "Indians not taxed," and added three-fifths of "all other Persons," meaning enslaved people, who could not vote, still added to the representation of the states that held them.

review.question: Why was the First Congress unable to start work on March 4, 1789?
review.answer: Too few members had arrived in New York; only 8 of 22 senators and 13 of 59 representatives were present, so neither chamber had a quorum until April 1 (House) and April 6 (Senate).

timeline.event: Delegates at the Constitutional Convention agree on a two-chamber legislature with equal state representation in the Senate.
The First Federal Congress is scheduled to convene at Federal Hall in New York City, but neither chamber has a quorum.
The House of Representatives achieves the first quorum.
The Senate achieves its first quorum and the electoral votes for president are counted.
Representative James Madison proposes constitutional amendments on the House floor.
Congress begins a ten-year residence in Philadelphia.
The Senate moves into the unfinished Capitol in Washington, D.C.
British troops set fire to the Capitol during the War of 1812.
Hiram Revels is sworn in as the first African American senator.
A federal law fixes the House at 433 seats, plus one each for Arizona and New Mexico on statehood.
The Seventeenth Amendment, providing for popular election of senators, is ratified.
The Senate adopts its first cloture rule to limit filibusters.
Hattie Caraway becomes the first woman elected to the Senate.
The Legislative Reorganization Act reforms the committee system.

misconception.myth: The Constitution fixes the House of Representatives at 435 members.
misconception.fact: The Constitution set only the House's first size (65 members) and a minimum of one representative per state; Congress set the number by law, enlarging the House after most censuses, fixing it at 433 plus two in 1911 and capping it at 435 from 1929, apart from a temporary 437 after Alaska and Hawaii joined.
misconception.why: Because 435 has not changed for about a century, it is easy to mistake an ordinary statute that Congress could amend for a constitutional rule.

title: United States Constitution
aliases: Constitution of the United States of America
summary: The supreme law of the United States, a four-page charter signed in Philadelphia on September 17, 1787, and ratified in 1788 that created the federal government of three separate branches, divided power between the nation and the states, and has been amended twenty-seven times.

review.question: How does the Constitution try to keep any one part of the government from becoming too powerful?
review.answer: It separates legislative, executive and judicial power among Congress, the president and the courts, gives each checks on the others such as the veto, veto override, Senate confirmation, impeachment and judicial review, and divides power between the national government and the states.

review.question: Why did several states ratify only after being promised amendments, and what came of that promise?
review.answer: Anti-Federalists feared a strong central government could threaten individual liberties and demanded a bill of rights; the First Congress proposed twelve amendments in September 1789, and ten were ratified on December 15, 1791, as the Bill of Rights.

review.question: How did the original Constitution protect slavery without using the word "slave"?
review.answer: It used euphemisms such as other persons and persons held to service or labor; it counted three-fifths of enslaved people for representation and taxes, barred Congress from banning their importation before 1808, and required the return of people who escaped slavery into another state.

review.question: How did Charles Beard's interpretation of the Constitution differ from that of later ideological historians?
review.answer: Beard argued in 1913 that the framers and ratifiers acted mainly to protect their economic interests, while historians such as Bernard Bailyn and Gordon Wood argued that political ideas, especially republicanism, better explain the framing; later scholarship has largely undermined Beard's account.

timeline.event: A quorum of seven states is finally present and the Federal Convention opens in the Pennsylvania State House.
Delegates sign the finished four-page Constitution in Philadelphia.
Delaware becomes the first state to ratify.
New Hampshire becomes the ninth state to ratify, enough for the Constitution to take effect.
The date the framers set for the new Congress to convene.
The Senate achieves its first quorum.
The First Congress proposes twelve amendments to the states.
Rhode Island becomes the thirteenth and last original state to ratify.
Ten of the twelve proposed amendments are ratified as the Bill of Rights.
A pay amendment proposed in 1789 is ratified as the Twenty-seventh Amendment.

misconception.myth: The Constitution declares that "all men are created equal."
misconception.fact: That phrase comes from the Declaration of Independence. The original Constitution contained no such promise and instead counted three-fifths of enslaved people for apportionment; an equality guarantee entered the text only with the Fourteenth Amendment after the Civil War.
misconception.why: Running the two founding documents together hides how the 1787 text accommodated slavery and how much the Reconstruction amendments changed it.

title: Voting Rights Act of 1965
summary: The federal statute, signed by President Lyndon B. Johnson on August 6, 1965, that enforced the Fifteenth Amendment by banning racial discrimination in voting nationwide, outlawing literacy tests, and placing jurisdictions with a record of disenfranchisement under federal registration and "preclearance" oversight.

review.question: Why did Congress single out certain states and counties for preclearance instead of relying only on lawsuits?
review.answer: Case-by-case litigation was slow and easily evaded, so Section 4 used a formula (a voting test or device in 1964 plus registration or turnout under 50 percent) to identify places with a record of disenfranchisement, and Section 5 required them to get federal approval before changing voting rules; the Supreme Court said this shifted the "advantage of time and inertia" from those discriminating to their victims.

review.question: How did the Selma campaign help produce the Act?
review.answer: Violence against peaceful marchers, especially on Bloody Sunday in March 1965, drew national outrage; Johnson sent voting rights proposals to Congress within days and later credited the events at Selma with prompting federal action, though he had already been considering reform after the 1964 election.

review.question: How did Shelby County v. Holder change the Act without striking down Section 5 itself?
review.answer: The Court held that the Section 4(b) coverage formula relied on decades-old data, so no jurisdiction could be required to seek preclearance until Congress wrote a new formula, which it has not done.

review.question: What did the 1982 amendment to Section 2 change, and why?
review.answer: After Mobile v. Bolden (1980) required proof of discriminatory purpose in vote-dilution cases, Congress amended Section 2 so a violation could be shown without proving intent.

timeline.event: Voting rights activist Jimmie Lee Jackson dies of a gunshot wound inflicted by a white man in Alabama, prompting calls for a march from Selma to Montgomery.
On "Bloody Sunday," law enforcement officers attack about 600 marchers leaving Selma for Montgomery.
President Johnson outlines his voting rights proposals in a televised address to a joint session of Congress.
Some 25,000 marchers led by Martin Luther King Jr. reach Montgomery under federal protection.
The Senate passes S. 1564, 77 to 19, a day after invoking cloture 70 to 30 to end a filibuster.
The House passes H.R. 6400, 333 to 85.
Johnson signs the Voting Rights Act at the Capitol, a day after Congress completed final passage.
In South Carolina v. Katzenbach the Supreme Court upholds the Act's constitutionality.
Congress extends Section 5 preclearance for five years.
Congress extends preclearance for seven years and adds protections for language-minority citizens.
Congress renews the special provisions for 25 years and amends Section 2 so plaintiffs need not prove discriminatory purpose, responding to Mobile v. Bolden (1980).

Congress renews the special provisions for 25 more years in the Fannie Lou Hamer, Rosa Parks, Coretta Scott King, Cesar E. Chavez, Barbara Jordan, William Velazquez and Dr. Hector Garcia reauthorization act.
In Shelby County v. Holder the Supreme Court, 5 to 4, holds the Section 4(b) coverage formula unconstitutional, halting preclearance.
In Louisiana v. Callais the Supreme Court, 6 to 3, holds that Section 2 imposes liability in redistricting only where evidence supports a strong inference of intentional discrimination.

misconception.myth: Black Americans' right to vote rests on the Voting Rights Act and will expire unless Congress renews the Act.
misconception.fact: The bans on racial discrimination in voting in the Fifteenth Amendment and in the Act's core provisions, such as Section 2, are permanent; only the "special provisions" for certain jurisdictions, such as Section 5 preclearance and federal examiners and observers, were written with expiration dates and periodically renewed.
misconception.why: The rumor, which the Justice Department publicly called false, confuses temporary remedies with the underlying constitutional right, and it can distract from the real debates over how the Act's remedies should work.

title: War in Afghanistan (2001–2021)
summary: The twenty-year U.S.-led war in Afghanistan, launched on October 7, 2001, after the September 11 attacks to destroy al Qaeda's base and topple the Taliban government that sheltered it, which ended with the Taliban's return to power and the final U.S. withdrawal from Kabul on August 30, 2021.

review.question: Why did the United States go to war in Afghanistan in 2001?
review.answer: After the September 11 attacks Congress authorized force against those who planned them and anyone who harbored them; al Qaeda was based in Afghanistan under Taliban protection, so U.S. strikes began on October 7, 2001, to destroy al Qaeda's base and drive the Taliban from power.

review.question: How did the war in Iraq affect the war in Afghanistan?
review.answer: From 2003 U.S. attention and resources shifted to Iraq, where about 150,000–170,000 U.S. troops served against about 20,000 in Afghanistan; officials later said Afghanistan was under-managed in those years as the Taliban regrouped and violence rose from about 2005–2006.

review.question: How did the 2020 Doha agreement contribute to the events of August 2021?
review.answer: It committed the United States to withdraw all forces within 14 months without conditioning that on reduced Taliban violence; Congressional researchers reported it demoralized Afghan forces, and the later departure of contractors who maintained aircraft and supplied air support helped the Afghan military collapse as the Taliban took Kabul on August 15, 2021.

timeline.event: Congress's Authorization for Use of Military Force against those responsible for the September 11 attacks, and those who harbored them, is approved.
U.S. air strikes begin against Taliban military installations and al Qaeda training camps.
Hamid Karzai's southern opposition forces and U.S. Marines take Kandahar after the Taliban abandon Kabul and the north.
NATO assumes command of the UN-mandated International Security Assistance Force (ISAF).
In a speech at West Point, President Obama approves a surge of 33,000 more U.S. troops, with withdrawals to begin in July 2011.
Navy SEALs kill Osama bin Laden at a compound near Abbottabad, Pakistan.
Afghan forces begin taking over security responsibility from international troops.
ISAF's combat mission having ended in late 2014, NATO's smaller train-and-advise Resolute Support mission begins.
The United States and the Taliban sign the Agreement for Bringing Peace to Afghanistan in Doha, Qatar, setting a 14-month withdrawal timeline.
President Biden announces a final withdrawal to begin May 1, later setting August 31 as the end of the military mission.
The Taliban enter Kabul and President Ashraf Ghani flees the country.
A suicide bombing claimed by the Islamic State affiliate at a Kabul airport gate kills 13 U.S. service members and dozens of Afghans.
The last U.S. forces leave Kabul, ending the U.S. military and diplomatic withdrawal.

misconception.myth: Afghanistan's army collapsed in 2021 simply because its soldiers would not fight.
misconception.fact: At least 66,000 Afghan troops were killed in the war (SIGAR, 2021), and Congressional researchers traced the collapse to structural causes — corruption that left soldiers unpaid or unfed, dependence on departing U.S. contractors for maintenance, intelligence and air support, overstretched rural outposts, and demoralization after the 2020 U.S.-Taliban agreement.
misconception.why: The speed of the Taliban's August 2021 advance made a single explanation tempting, but it hides two decades of heavy Afghan losses and the design choices that left the force unable to sustain itself once foreign support ended.
